items.stem: What is the reward to the factor of production land?
items.answer: Rent
items.markingKey: Land → rent; labour → wages; capital → interest; enterprise → profit.

items.stem: Explain the difference between capital and enterprise as factors of production.
items.answer: Capital is man-made goods (machines, buildings) used to produce other goods; enterprise is the willingness and ability to organise the other factors and take risks in production.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capital definition; 1 mark: enterprise definition [2]

items.stem: Explain why the quality of labour, not only its quantity, matters for an economy’s output.
items.answer: Better educated, trained and healthier workers are more productive, so the same number of workers can produce more output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: quality = skills/health; 1 mark: higher productivity/output [2]

items.stem: The computers used by software engineers at Cobalt Group. Which factor of production is this?
items.answer: Capital
items.markingKey: Capital: man-made equipment used in production; earns interest.

items.stem: Sofia, who designs and launches a new app and takes the financial risk. Which factor of production is this? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Enterprise: innovation and risk-bearing; earns profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Enterprise; 1 mark: explanation – innovation and risk-bearing; earns profit. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Apex Ltd makes televisions in Doha. Five years ago it employed 30 craft workers who each made complete products. It now employs 18 workers on a production line, each doing one task, with new machinery. Monthly output has risen from 400 to 700 units. The founder, Tomás, says the change was a risk because she borrowed heavily to buy the machines. (a) Calculate output per worker before and after the change. (b) Explain the risk taken by the founder as an entrepreneur.
items.answer: (a) 13.3 → 38.9 units (b) Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital.
items.markingKey: (a) 400/30 and 700/18 [2] (b) Credit: Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital. [2]

items.stem: What is the reward to enterprise?
items.answer: Profit
items.markingKey: Entrepreneurs bear risk and receive profit.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why labour may be geographically immobile.
items.answer: Differences in housing costs between regions, family and social ties, cost of moving, lack of information about jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason explained [2]

items.stem: Explain why money is not regarded as a factor of production.
items.answer: Money cannot itself produce goods; it is a means of buying the factors (e.g. capital equipment) that do.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: money not productive; 1 mark: used to acquire factors [2]

items.stem: Many skilled nurses have emigrated from Sundara. Explain how this affects the quantity and quality of labour in Sundara.
items.answer: The labour force is smaller and the average level of skill falls, reducing productive potential, especially in healthcare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: quantity falls; 1 mark: quality/skills fall [2]

items.stem: In one year Chloe earns $30,000 as a teacher, receives $3,000 from renting out a field, earns 2% interest on $40,000 lent to a business and makes $12,000 profit from a small online shop. Calculate the income earned from capital.
items.markingKey: 2% × 40,000 = $800 (interest is the reward to capital).

items.stem: Identify the factor of production in each case and state its reward. (i) The river water used to cool a power station in Istrana. (ii) Mei, who risks her savings to start a restaurant meals business.
items.answer: (i) Land (ii) Enterprise
items.markingKey: (i) Land – a natural resource. [2] (ii) Enterprise – organises factors and bears risk; earns profit. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Esteria has few natural resources but has invested heavily in education. Explain the four factors of production and the reward each one earns.
items.answer: Land (natural resources) → rent; labour (human effort) → wages; capital (man-made aids) → interest; enterprise (organisation, risk) → profit; quantity and quality.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Land (natural resources) → rent; labour (human effort) → wages; capital (man-made aids) → interest; enterprise (organisation, risk) → profit; quantity and quality. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the division of labour?
options: Allocating workers between firms by the government
Breaking down production into separate tasks, each carried out by different workers
Dividing workers into skilled and unskilled groups
items.answer: Breaking down production into separate tasks, each carried out by different workers
items.markingKey: Workers specialise in particular tasks.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why the division of labour increases labour productivity.
items.answer: Workers become skilled through repetition; less time is lost moving between tasks; it allows use of specialised machinery; workers can be matched to tasks they are best at.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why a high degree of specialisation can make a firm vulnerable.
items.answer: Production depends on every stage; if one group of workers is absent or on strike, the whole process stops.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: interdependence; 1 mark: disruption halts production [2]

items.stem: At Borealis plc, 4 workers each make complete shirts, producing 5 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 40 shirts a day. Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker.

At Redwood Corp, 6 workers each make complete tables, producing 6 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 54 tables a day. Each worker is paid $60 a day. (a) Calculate output per worker and the labour cost per unit before and after. (b) Explain why output per worker rose. (c) Explain one possible drawback of the change for Redwood Corp.
items.answer: (a) Output per worker 6 → 9; labour cost per unit $10 → $6.67. (b) Workers become quicker and more skilled at one task, no time lost switching tasks, specialist tools. (c) Boredom/low motivation, absenteeism or disruption if one stage stops.
items.markingKey: (a) output per worker both [1]; cost per unit 60/6 and 60/9 [2] (b) reason [1] (c) drawback [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: Borealis plc makes smartphones in Jakarta. Five years ago it employed 40 craft workers who each made complete products. It now employs 25 workers on a production line, each doing one task, with new machinery. Monthly output has risen from 400 to 700 units. The founder, Omar, says the change was a risk because she borrowed heavily to buy the machines. (a) Identify two factors of production mentioned in the extract and their rewards. (b) Explain the risk taken by the founder as an entrepreneur.
items.answer: (a) Labour (workers) → wages; capital (machinery) → interest; enterprise (the founder) → profit. (b) Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each factor with reward [2] (b) Credit: Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital. [2]

items.stem: Explain why money is important for specialisation in an economy.
items.answer: Money acts as a medium of exchange, removing the need for a double coincidence of wants, so specialists can easily sell their output and buy what they need.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: medium of exchange; 1 mark: removes barter problem, enables trade [2]

items.stem: Zentara specialises in producing paper for export. Explain one risk to Zentara of this specialisation.
items.answer: If world demand or price for paper falls, incomes and jobs in Zentara fall sharply because it depends heavily on one product.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dependence; 1 mark: effect of a fall in demand/price [2]

items.stem: Sundara specialises in producing laptops for export. Explain one risk to Sundara of this specialisation.
items.answer: If world demand or price for laptops falls, incomes and jobs in Sundara fall sharply because it depends heavily on one product.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dependence; 1 mark: effect of a fall in demand/price [2]

items.stem: At Orchid Ltd, 8 workers each make complete tables, producing 4 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 80 tables a day. Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker.

At Fenwick & Co, 6 workers each make complete pairs of shoes, producing 5 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 48 pairs of shoes a day. Each worker is paid $60 a day. (a) Calculate output per worker and the labour cost per unit before and after. (b) Explain why output per worker rose. (c) Explain one possible drawback of the change for Fenwick & Co.
items.answer: (a) Output per worker 5 → 8; labour cost per unit $12 → $7.50. (b) Workers become quicker and more skilled at one task, no time lost switching tasks, specialist tools. (c) Boredom/low motivation, absenteeism or disruption if one stage stops.
items.markingKey: (a) output per worker both [1]; cost per unit 60/5 and 60/8 [2] (b) reason [1] (c) drawback [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain how the division of labour can increase productivity.
items.answer: Skill through repetition, time saving, use of specialist machinery, matching aptitudes; leads to lower unit costs; requires a large enough market and exchange.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Skill through repetition, time saving, use of specialist machinery, matching aptitudes; leads to lower unit costs; requires a large enough market and exchange. items.stem: What is the main role of the entrepreneur?
options: To set prices for the government
To supply labour in return for wages
To organise the other factors of production and bear the risk of the business
items.answer: To organise the other factors of production and bear the risk of the business
items.markingKey: Organising, decision-making, risk-bearing, innovation.

items.stem: Why is profit regarded as a reward for enterprise?
options: It is the same as interest on capital
It is fixed by contract like wages
It compensates the entrepreneur for bearing uninsurable risk
It is guaranteed by the government
items.answer: It compensates the entrepreneur for bearing uninsurable risk
items.markingKey: Uncertainty cannot be insured, so profit rewards risk-bearing.

items.stem: Explain why entrepreneurs are important for economic growth.
items.answer: They bring new products and production methods to market, create firms and jobs and raise productivity through innovation, increasing the economy’s productive capacity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: innovation/new firms; 1 mark: link to output/growth [2]

items.stem: Ravi runs a business selling rice. In one month Ravi sells 800 units at $12 each. Variable costs are $7.2 per unit and fixed costs are $4,000. Ravi gave up a job paying $3,500 a month to run the business. Calculate the monthly accounting profit.

The founder, Hana, says the change was a risk because she borrowed heavily to buy the machines. (a) Calculate output per worker before and after the change. (b) Explain the risk taken by the founder as an entrepreneur.
items.answer: (a) 15 → 48 units (b) Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital.
items.markingKey: (a) 600/40 and 1200/25 [2] (b) Credit: Borrowing to buy machines commits the firm to interest payments; if demand falls she may make losses and lose her capital. [2]

items.stem: Kwame runs a business selling gym memberships. In one month Kwame sells 1,500 units at $12 each. Variable costs are $6 per unit and fixed costs are $2,000. Kwame gave up a job paying $3,000 a month to run the business. Calculate the monthly accounting profit.

Diego runs a business selling running shoes. In one month Diego sells 1,200 units at $4 each. Variable costs are $2.4 per unit and fixed costs are $4,000. Diego gave up a job paying $3,500 a month to run the business. (a) Calculate the monthly profit. (b) Taking into account the opportunity cost of the job given up, explain whether running the business is worthwhile. (c) Explain why profit is the reward for the risk taken by Diego.
items.answer: (a) −$2,080 (b) After deducting the forgone salary of $3,500 the gain is −$5,580: not worthwhile in money terms, it earns less than the job forgone (unless non-money benefits or future growth justify it). (c) Revenue is uncertain; profit compensates for the uninsurable risk of loss.
items.markingKey: (a) TR − TC = −2080 [2] (b) compares with $3,500 forgone [1]; conclusion [1] (c) uncertainty/risk [1] [5]

items.stem: Kenji runs a business selling concert tickets. In one month Kenji sells 1,200 units at $5 each. Variable costs are $2 per unit and fixed costs are $2,000. Kenji gave up a job paying $2,500 a month to run the business. (a) Calculate the monthly profit. (b) Taking into account the opportunity cost of the job given up, explain whether running the business is worthwhile. (c) Explain why profit is the reward for the risk taken by Kenji.
items.answer: (a) $1,600 (b) After deducting the forgone salary of $2,500 the gain is −$900: not worthwhile in money terms, it earns less than the job forgone (unless non-money benefits or future growth justify it). (c) Revenue is uncertain; profit compensates for the uninsurable risk of loss.
items.markingKey: (a) TR − TC = 1600 [2] (b) compares with $2,500 forgone [1]; conclusion [1] (c) uncertainty/risk [1] [5]

options: Money saved in a bank account
A delivery van used by a firm
items.answer: A delivery van used by a firm
items.markingKey: Capital = man-made goods used to produce other goods and services.

items.answer: The labour force is smaller and the average level of skill falls, reducing productive potential, especially in healthcare.

items.stem: Copper deposits being mined in Marvona. Which factor of production is this?
items.answer: Land

items.stem: Newspapers in Tarvia have recently reported a lively debate among economists on this issue. (a) Explain how the division of labour can increase productivity. (b) ‘The benefits of specialisation outweigh its drawbacks for workers and firms.’ Evaluate this view.
items.answer: (a) Skill through repetition, time saving, use of specialist machinery, matching aptitudes; leads to lower unit costs; requires a large enough market and exchange. items.stem: Explain the difference between insurable and uninsurable risk faced by an entrepreneur.
items.answer: Insurable risks (fire, theft) can be statistically predicted and covered by insurance; uninsurable risks (changes in demand, new competitors) cannot, and profit is the reward for bearing them.

items.stem: Explain why some entrepreneurs continue in business even when making a loss for a period.
items.answer: They expect future profits, e.g. once the brand is established or demand recovers; they may value independence or have sunk costs.

items.stem: At Orchid Ltd, 6 workers each make complete bicycles, producing 4 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 60 bicycles a day. Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker.

At Fenwick & Co, 5 workers each make complete chairs, producing 5 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 50 chairs a day. Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker.

At Tidewater plc, 8 workers each make complete bicycles, producing 3 a day each. After reorganising so each worker specialises in one task, the team makes 36 bicycles a day. Each worker is paid $50 a day. (a) Calculate output per worker and the labour cost per unit before and after. (b) Explain why output per worker rose. (c) Explain one possible drawback of the change for Tidewater plc.
items.answer: (a) Output per worker 3 → 4.5; labour cost per unit $16.67 → $11.11. (b) Workers become quicker and more skilled at one task, no time lost switching tasks, specialist tools. (c) Boredom/low motivation, absenteeism or disruption if one stage stops.
items.markingKey: (a) output per worker both [1]; cost per unit 50/3 and 50/4.5 [2] (b) reason [1] (c) drawback [1] [5]

items.stem: A policy institute in Seoul has published a report on this issue for the government of Fendaria. (a) Explain how the division of labour can increase productivity. (b) Consider whether the benefits of specialisation outweigh its drawbacks for workers and firms.
items.answer: (a) Skill through repetition, time saving, use of specialist machinery, matching aptitudes; leads to lower unit costs; requires a large enough market and exchange. (b) For: Higher productivity, lower costs, higher wages and competitiveness. Against: Boredom, alienation, deskilling, interdependence and disruption, structural unemployment risk; depends on job design and the market. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Indicative content: Skill through repetition, time saving, use of specialist machinery, matching aptitudes; leads to lower unit costs; requires a large enough market and exchange. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8] (b) Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Higher productivity, lower costs, higher wages and competitiveness. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Boredom, alienation, deskilling, interdependence and disruption, structural unemployment risk; depends on job design and the market. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: Which characteristic is most associated with entrepreneurs?
options: Willingness to take risks and innovate
items.answer: Willingness to take risks and innovate
items.markingKey: Enterprise involves risk-taking and new ideas.

items.stem: The government of Halvoria offers start-up loans to young entrepreneurs. Explain why it might do this.
items.answer: To encourage new firms, jobs, innovation and competition; entrepreneurs often lack access to finance because banks see them as risky.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefits of enterprise; 1 mark: finance barrier [2]

items.stem: Zara leaves a salaried job to open a fresh fruit shop in Karachi. Explain the risks Zara is taking as an entrepreneur.
items.answer: Loss of a secure salary (opportunity cost), risk of losing invested savings if demand is too low or costs too high; income is uncertain profit rather than fixed wages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forgone salary; 1 mark: uncertain profit/loss of capital [2]

items.stem: Sipho runs a business selling concert tickets. In one month Sipho sells 1,200 units at $10 each. Variable costs are $6 per unit and fixed costs are $2,000. Sipho gave up a job paying $2,500 a month to run the business. Calculate the monthly accounting profit.

Extract: Quarry Bay Ltd makes chocolate bars in Kuala Lumpur. Five years ago it employed 20 craft workers who each made complete products. It now employs 12 workers on a production line, each doing one task, with new machinery. Monthly output has risen from 500 to 900 units. The founder, Lina, says the change was a risk because she borrowed heavily to buy the machines. (a) Calculate output per worker before and after the change. (b) Identify two factors of production mentioned in the extract and their rewards.
items.answer: (a) 25 → 75 units (b) Labour (workers) → wages; capital (machinery) → interest; enterprise (the founder) → profit.
items.markingKey: (a) 500/20 and 900/12 [2] (b) 1 mark each factor with reward [2]
